title: Cartesian simplicial model of marked simplicial sets over a point
statement:
Fix nested universes as in [def-weil-size-convention] and simplicial sets, quasicategories, equivalences, functor simplicial sets and cores as in [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones]. A marked simplicial set is a pair $(X,M)$ with $M\subseteq X_1$ containing every degenerate edge; maps preserve marked edges. Products have an edge marked exactly when both its coordinates are marked. Write $K^\flat$ for marking only degenerate edges, $K^\sharp$ for marking every edge, and $C^\natural$ for marking exactly the equivalences in a quasicategory $C$. The marked internal Hom $Y^X$ is specified by $\operatorname{Hom}(Z,Y^X)=\operatorname{Hom}(Z\times X,Y)$; define
$$\operatorname{Map}^{\sharp}(X,Y)_n=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{sSet}^+}(X\times(\Delta^n)^\sharp,Y).$$
There is a combinatorial simplicial model structure on marked simplicial sets over a point. Cofibrations are the maps injective on underlying simplices. A map $f:X\to Y$ is a weak equivalence precisely when $\operatorname{Map}^{\sharp}(Y,C^\natural)\to\operatorname{Map}^{\sharp}(X,C^\natural)$ is a weak homotopy equivalence for every small quasicategory $C$; fibrations are the maps with the right lifting property against cofibrations that are weak equivalences. Its fibrant objects are precisely the $C^\natural$. Here a model structure is on a complete and cocomplete category and has retract-closed weak equivalences satisfying two-out-of-three and functorial weak factorization systems (cofibration, trivial fibration) and (trivial cofibration, fibration); trivial means also a weak equivalence. A weak factorization system consists of factorizations and the mutually characterized diagonal-lifting classes. Combinatorial means that both systems are generated by sets and the category is locally presentable, namely cocomplete and generated, for some regular cardinal $\kappa$, under $\kappa$-filtered colimits by a small set of objects whose Hom functors preserve $\kappa$-filtered colimits. Simplicial means enriched, tensored and cotensored over simplicial sets with the Kan model structure of [lem-coef-kan-quillen-right-proper], with mapping objects $\operatorname{Map}^{\sharp}$, tensor $X\otimes K=X\times K^\sharp$, and the pushout-product lifting axiom.

Every object is cofibrant, the terminal object is $(\Delta^0)^\sharp$, and the cartesian pushout product of two cofibrations is a cofibration, trivial if either factor is trivial. For $i:X\to X'$ and $j:Y\to Y'$ this pushout product is $(X'\times Y)\amalg_{X\times Y}(X\times Y')\to X'\times Y'$. Products with any marked simplicial set preserve weak equivalences. For quasicategories $C,D$ there is a natural identity
$$\operatorname{Map}^{\sharp}(C^\natural,D^\natural)=\operatorname{Fun}(C,D)^\simeq.$$
Consequently the simplicial category of fibrant objects, with this Kan enrichment, has homotopy coherent nerve equal to $\mathrm{Cat}_\infty$, modeled as the coherent nerve of small quasicategories with these mapping Kan complexes; the coherent nerve convention is [lem-coef-coherent-nerve-comparison]. The identifications respect composition. The weak equivalence and fibrant-object assertions are unchanged on enlarging the universe; the structure, small colimits and its functorial replacement constructions can be formed in the universe of the input simplicial sets.

source.place: Definition 3.0.0.1; Definition 3.1.0.1; internal Homs preceding Remark 3.1.3.1 and Proposition 3.1.3.3; Proposition 3.1.3.7; Proposition 3.1.4.1; Proposition 3.1.4.2 and Corollaries 3.1.4.3-3.1.4.4. The point case marks precisely equivalences, as explained in Remark 3.1.4.6. Universe stability is the universe-relative version of these constructions. Read online 2026-10-16; not archived under literature/. No Stacks tag states this infinity-categorical theorem.

proof.text: Limits of marked sets are underlying limits with an edge marked when all projections are marked; colimits are underlying colimits with the images of marked edges marked. These formulas give all small limits and colimits. Every marked set is the filtered union of its finite subobjects, where finite means finitely many nondegenerate simplices. A map from a finite subobject into a filtered colimit factors at one stage, including each of its finitely many marked-edge conditions; equality of two such maps is likewise witnessed at one stage. There is a small set of finite marked simplicial sets up to isomorphism. Thus this category is locally finitely presentable. Monomorphisms are generated, by adjoining nondegenerate simplices in increasing dimension and then additional marked edges, by $I=\{(\partial\Delta^n)^\flat\to(\Delta^n)^\flat\}_{n\geq0}\cup\{(\Delta^1)^\flat\to(\Delta^1)^\sharp\}$. In the simplex-adjoining stage retain exactly the source markings; mark the remaining edges in the second stage. Pushouts, transfinite composites and retracts of these maps are still degreewise injective, so their weakly saturated closure is exactly the desired cofibrations.

source.place: Section 3.1.3, marked-category setup; direct degreewise and finite-presentation argument for the point case of Proposition 3.1.3.7.

proof.text:
Let $W$ be the class in the statement. The saturation lemma proves that $W$ is perfect. The marked-anodyne calculus gives Kan mapping objects $\operatorname{Map}^\sharp(X,C^
atural)$, Kan restriction fibrations along cofibrations, and trivial restriction fibrations along marked-anodyne maps. In particular marked-anodyne maps belong to $W$. If $w:X	o Y$ belongs to $W$ and $X\hookrightarrow X'$ is a cofibration, mapping its pushout square into $C^
atural$ gives a pullback square of Kan complexes. The pullback leg $\operatorname{Map}^\sharp(X',C^
atural)	o\operatorname{Map}^\sharp(X,C^
atural)$ is a Kan fibration. Right properness therefore says the new restriction map is a weak homotopy equivalence. This proves pushout stability of $W$ along cofibrations.

An $I$-injective map $p:X\to Y$ is an underlying trivial Kan fibration and satisfies: an edge of $X$ is marked exactly when its image is marked. The first assertion follows from boundary lifting, since every underlying boundary square can be given minimal markings; the second follows by lifting against $(\Delta^1)^\flat\to(\Delta^1)^\sharp$. Choose an underlying section $s$ by lifting against $\varnothing\to Y$. It preserves markings by the second assertion. The same assertion makes every underlying map to $X$ over $Y$ marking-preserving when its composite with $p$ is so. The inclusion $X\times\partial\Delta^1\hookrightarrow X\times\Delta^1$ is an underlying monomorphism. Lift its endpoint maps $sp$ and $\mathrm{id}_X$ against $p$, with base map the projection to $Y$, to obtain a marked homotopy $X\times(\Delta^1)^\sharp\to X$. Precomposition gives homotopy inverse maps on every Kan mapping complex into $C^\natural$, hence $p\in W$. Apply the perfect-class recognition lemma with this $I$, the locally presentable category of step 1, and the pushout stability of step 2. It supplies a left proper combinatorial model structure and both functorial weak factorization systems with the stated classes.

source.place: Proposition 3.1.3.7, proof (3); Proposition A.2.6.15. The section and homotopy lift are explicit.

proof.text:
The marked-anodyne calculus gives $j:X	o Q^
atural$ marked anodyne. If $X$ is fibrant in the model structure of step 3, $j$ is a trivial cofibration and has a retraction $r:Q^
atural	o X$. Lifting properties are closed under retracts: a square for a retract is included into the original square, filled there, and projected back. Thus $X	o*$ has the marked-anodyne lifting property and the calculus identifies $X=C^
atural$. Conversely, let $X=C^
atural$ and let $i:A	o B$ be any trivial cofibration. Restriction on $\operatorname{Map}^\sharp(-,X)$ is a Kan fibration by the calculus and a weak equivalence by the definition of $W$; hence it is a trivial Kan fibration and is surjective on vertices. Every map $A	o X$ therefore extends to $B$, proving fibrancy. Finally $\varnothing	o X$ is always a cofibration and the terminal marked set is $(\Delta^0)^\sharp$, directly from the definitions.

source.place: Proposition 3.1.4.1; direct argument using Lemma 3.1.3.6 avoids any unmentioned rectification lemma.

proof.text:
For natural quasicategories, a weak equivalence $f:C^
atural	o D^
atural$ has an inverse up to paths in the sharp mapping complexes: Surjectivity of $\pi_0\operatorname{Map}^\sharp(D^
atural,C^
atural)	o\pi_0\operatorname{Map}^\sharp(C^
atural,C^
atural)$ gives a marked map $g:D^
atural	o C^
atural$ with $gf\simeq\mathrm{id}_C$. Postcomposition with $f$ gives $fgf\simeq f$. Injectivity of $\pi_0\operatorname{Map}^\sharp(D^
atural,D^
atural)	o\pi_0\operatorname{Map}^\sharp(C^
atural,D^
atural)$ then gives $fg\simeq\mathrm{id}_D$, since the images of $fg$ and $\mathrm{id}_D$ are $fgf$ and $f$. These components contain edge paths since the mapping complexes are Kan. Conversely such an inverse gives homotopy inverse maps on every testing mapping complex, hence a weak equivalence. The homotopies remain marked homotopies after multiplying by any marked $Z$, so $f	imes\mathrm{id}_Z\in W$. For an arbitrary $f:X	o Y$ in $W$, choose marked-anodyne $X	o C^
atural$ and then marked-anodyne $C^
atural\amalg_XY	o D^
atural$. The induced $Y	o D^
atural$ is marked anodyne as a composite of a pushout and a marked-anodyne map. Two-out-of-three shows $C^
atural	o D^
atural$ is in $W$. Multiplication by $Z$ preserves the other two maps because their products are pushout products with $\varnothing	o Z$, and are marked anodyne by the calculus. Two-out-of-three now proves $f	imes\mathrm{id}_Z\in W$ in general.

source.place: Proposition 3.1.4.2; point-case inverse argument of Proposition 3.1.3.5 written out.

proof.text: For cofibrations $i:X\hookrightarrow X'$ and $j:Y\hookrightarrow Y'$, their pushout product is the inclusion of the degreewise union $(X'\times Y)\cup_{X\times Y}(X\times Y')$ into $X'\times Y'$, so it is a cofibration, also when a map adds only markings. Suppose $i\in W$. The map $X\times Y\to X'\times Y$ belongs to $W$ by step 5; push it out along the cofibration $X\times Y\to X\times Y'$ to obtain a weak equivalence $X\times Y'\to (X'\times Y)\amalg_{X\times Y}(X\times Y')$ by left properness from step 3. Its composite to $X'\times Y'$ is $i\times\mathrm{id}_{Y'}$, again in $W$. Two-out-of-three proves that the pushout product is trivial. If $j\in W$, the already proved case applied to $(j,i)$ makes $j\mathbin\square i$ trivial. The coordinate switches on all four products induce an isomorphism of arrows $i\mathbin\square j\cong j\mathbin\square i$; they preserve markings because the product marking condition is symmetric. Isomorphisms belong to $W$ and two-out-of-three therefore gives the assertion for $i\mathbin\square j$.

source.place: Corollary 3.1.4.3; deduction from steps 3 and 5 written out, with the correctly typed pushout-product formula.

proof.text: To construct the marked internal Hom $Y^X$, take its underlying simplicial set to have $n$-simplices the marked maps $X\times(\Delta^n)^\flat\to Y$, with operators given by restriction. Mark an edge precisely when its map $X\times(\Delta^1)^\flat\to Y$ also preserves the additional markings of $X\times(\Delta^1)^\sharp$. Degenerate edges satisfy this condition. Under the underlying exponential bijection, a map $Z\to Y^X$ preserves markings precisely when evaluation carries every pair of a marked edge of $Z$ and a marked edge of $X$ to a marked edge of $Y$. This is exactly the condition for $Z\times X\to Y$ to preserve markings, proving the marked exponential adjunction. The sharp mapping formula defines composition by the diagonal on the simplex parameter and evaluation; associativity and units are those of composition of marked maps. The tensor is $X\times K^\sharp$. Its cotensor is the marked internal Hom $Y^{K^\sharp}$, because $(-)^\sharp$ preserves products: in degree $n$, the cotensor adjunction identifies marked maps $X\times(\Delta^n)^\sharp\times K^\sharp\to Y$ with maps $K\times\Delta^n\to\operatorname{Map}^\sharp(X,Y)$. The tensor adjunction follows from the same identity with the $X$ and $K$ variables grouped together. For a trivial cofibration $j:K\hookrightarrow L$ of Kan-model simplicial sets and a quasicategory $C$, all edges of the parameter are marked, so $\operatorname{Map}^\sharp(K^\sharp,C^\natural)=\operatorname{Fun}(K,C^\simeq)$. Restriction to $K$ is a trivial Kan fibration: a boundary lifting problem adjoints to a lift of $C^\simeq\to*$ against a pushout product of a boundary inclusion with $j$, which is anodyne by the cited unmarked pushout-product lemma. Therefore $j^\sharp$ belongs to $W$. For a cofibration $i$ of marked sets and a cofibration $j$ of unmarked simplicial sets, the simplicial pushout product is $i\mathbin\square j^\sharp$. Step 6 makes it a cofibration, trivial when $i$ is trivial or when $j$ is trivial by the preceding test. This is the simplicial model axiom; the sharp parameter is essential.

source.place: Corollary 3.1.4.4; the unmarked mapping-space claim is proved by lifting and pushout products. Internal Homs preceding Remark 3.1.3.1.

proof.text:
For quasicategories $C,D$, the underlying simplicial set $\operatorname{Map}^ lat(C^
atural,D^
atural)$ is $\operatorname{Fun}(C,D)$: a map $C	imes\Delta^n	o D$ automatically preserves the marked edges of $C^
atural	imes(\Delta^n)^ lat$, since these are equivalences in a fixed $C$-slice. The marked-anodyne calculus identifies its sharp mapping subset with its core, giving the claimed natural identity. Concretely the extra condition is that the transformations at every vertex of $C$ have equivalence components; the pointwise equivalence criterion gives exactly the equivalence edges in $\operatorname{Fun}(C,D)$. For a diagonal product edge, the two triangles in the product express its image as the composite of its two coordinate images, so this vertexwise condition also checks all marked product edges. Restriction and composition act by the same maps on both sides, so the identity respects composition. The fibrant enriched category therefore has exactly the objects and mapping Kan complexes in the specified model for $\mathrm{Cat}_\infty$. Its coherent nerve is that model, using the cited coherent-nerve convention, and is a quasicategory because its mapping sets are Kan.

source.place: Definition 3.0.0.1; Remark 3.1.3.1; Proposition 1.2.7.3; coherent-nerve comparison for locally Kan simplicial categories.

proof.text: Fibrancy is the quasicategory condition with exactly the equivalence edges marked, and both are unchanged by universe enlargement: each is tested by finite simplices and inverse witnesses. To compare weak equivalences, apply the saturation functor of the cited lemma in the smaller universe. Its units pass the mapping tests in every larger universe, while $T(f)$ lies between naturally marked smaller quasicategories. Step 5 identifies the weak-equivalence test for $T(f)$ with existence of a functor inverse and coherent inverse homotopies. An inverse uses maps between the fixed smaller simplicial sets and finite simplex witnesses, so its existence is independent of the testing universe. Two-out-of-three with the units proves universe independence for $f$. Small colimits are the explicit degreewise colimits of step 1. The small generators, marked-anodyne replacements, finite saturation, and the recognition theorem's factorizations can each be used in the universe containing their input. Thus no inaccessible enlargement is needed to produce replacement objects, while the collection of all objects and its coherent nerve are taken in the larger ambient universe.
